points: Thomas Cresap was born around 1694.
Thomas Cresap held the rank of colonel.
Cresap was born in Skipton, Yorkshire, England.
Cresap was a settler in Maryland and Pennsylvania.
Cresap was a trader.
Cresap acted as Lord Baltimore's agent in the Maryland–Pennsylvania boundary dispute.
The Maryland–Pennsylvania boundary dispute in which Cresap served Lord Baltimore became known as Cresap's War.
Cresap and the Native American chief Nemacolin improved an existing Native American path to the Ohio Valley.
Cresap eventually settled near Cumberland, Maryland.
Cresap became a large landowner.
The article's introduction connects Cresap to further disputes near what is now Brownsville, Pennsylvania, including the French and Indian War and Lord Dunmore's War.
Cresap emigrated to the Maryland colony at age 15.
Cresap listed his occupation as carpenter in 1723.
Cresap first settled at the mouth of the Susquehanna River on Chesapeake Bay.
Cresap's first settlement was at the lower end of the Conejohela Valley floodplain.
Cresap built boats at his first settlement.
Cresap married Hannah Johnson in 1725.
Hannah Johnson's father was Thomas Johnson.
Thomas Johnson had Mount Johnson Island surveyed for himself on March 24, 1725.
Mount Johnson Island was at Peach Bottom Ferry.
Cresap traveled to Virginia at least once.
Claiborne, a Virginia-based trader, traded for furs in the lower Susquehanna area of Chesapeake Bay.
Cresap fled Virginia.
One account attributes Cresap's flight from Virginia to Native American raids against white settlers in 1722.
Another account says that a dozen or more fellow settlers drove Cresap away.
In the account involving other settlers, Cresap had been clearing timber to build a dwelling and secure his land claim.
In defending himself from the settlers, Cresap struck one assailant with a broad-ax.
After returning to Maryland, Cresap obtained a patent from Lord Baltimore to operate a ferry across the Susquehanna.
The ferry was at the head of tidal waters on the Susquehanna.
Captain John Smith traveled up Chesapeake Bay in 1608 and may have reached the area of the ferry.
Virginia had ceded the area of the ferry to Maryland.
Pennsylvania also claimed the area of the ferry under land grants to William Penn.
Cresap had little formal education.
Cresap became a land surveyor.
Cresap helped Lord Baltimore extend Maryland's western boundary due north from the source of the South Branch of the Potomac.
According to the article, the extension of the western boundary added at least one-third more territory to Maryland.
Cresap came to the Conejohela Valley in March 1730.
Cresap built a blockhouse on the banks of the Susquehanna.
The blockhouse stood three and a half miles downstream from present-day Wrightsville, near the site of Leber's Mill.
In 1730, Cresap obtained a Maryland patent for several hundred acres near the river at the blockhouse site for Blue Rock Ferry.
Cresap was commissioned a justice of the peace for Baltimore County in 1731.
While living on the lower Susquehanna, Cresap visited fertile valleys 30 miles farther upriver along its right bank.
The valleys Cresap visited are now in Hellam and Lower Windsor townships.
Cresap reported what he found in the upriver valleys to Lord Baltimore.
As early as 1721, Lord Baltimore considered extending Maryland's northern boundary on the west side of the Susquehanna to the northern limits of the 40th degree of latitude.
A few Maryland settlers gradually moved into the Conejohela Valley.
The Maryland settlers acted aggressively toward nearby Pennsylvania settlers.
Lord Baltimore did not make a practice of buying land from Native Americans.
Maryland settlers forcibly drove Native Americans from the disputed area.
Maryland settlers treated Native Americans on the west side of the Susquehanna cruelly.
The Maryland settlers initially lacked anyone able to hold the land they had taken from Native Americans or Pennsylvanians.
Pennsylvanians were determined to prevent Lord Baltimore from gaining a foothold in the disputed area.
The Conejohela Flats are in the lower Susquehanna Valley south of Wright's Ferry.
Cresap became notorious in the Conejohela Flats.
The actions of Cresap and his men on Lord Baltimore's behalf made Cresap a wanted criminal in Pennsylvania.
Cresap and his men repeatedly used force to evict settlers from disputed land.
The evicted settlers considered their occupation legal under Pennsylvania's colonial charter.
Cresap and Lord Baltimore considered the evicted settlers squatters on land covered by Maryland's charter.
Bloodshed during Cresap's War prompted King George II to issue an edict forcing a settlement of the boundary dispute.
The forced settlement went against Lord Baltimore's claims.
Cresap was regarded as a villain in Pennsylvania.
Cresap was regarded as something of a hero in Maryland.
Maryland has municipalities named after Cresap.
In 1735, Cresap obtained a Maryland patent for a group of islands at Blue Rock Ferry.
The islands were called the Isles of Promise.
There were several unsuccessful attempts to capture Cresap.
Pennsylvania Sheriff Samuel Smith captured Cresap on November 25, 1736.
Smith was accompanied by 24 armed men when he captured Cresap.
Hannah Cresap fought alongside her husband when he was captured.
At the time of Cresap's capture, he and Hannah had at least two and possibly three children.
Their eldest child was about nine at the time of Cresap's capture.
Pennsylvania authorities imprisoned Cresap after his capture.
While Cresap was imprisoned, Hannah and the children lived with Cresap's cousin Daniel Lowe.
Daniel Lowe drove a German settler out of his home in Grist Valley, also called Kreutz Creek, near Codorus.
Cresap was released around 1738.
After his release, Cresap moved beyond the frontier into the Potomac River watershed.
Cresap obtained a patent for about 2,000 acres along Antietam Creek in Maryland.
Cresap established a store and trading post on Antietam Creek to trade with Native Americans.
Cresap accumulated a large quantity of furs and pelts.
Cresap shipped his furs and pelts to England.
French privateers captured the ship carrying Cresap's furs and pelts.
Cresap lost the entire shipment.
Cresap received a grant of 400 acres in 1739.
Cresap named the 400-acre tract Long Meadows.
Cresap is said to have built a stone-and-log fort over a spring near Marsh Run.
Cresap moved farther west to within two miles of present-day Cumberland.
Cresap resumed trading with Native Americans near present-day Cumberland.
The Cumberland Narrows pass led into the Monongahela River valley.
In the 1740s, colonists petitioned the Crown for lands held by Native Americans in the Ohio Country across the Allegheny Mountains.
The Cumberland Narrows is one of only five navigable routes across the Appalachian barrier range.
Cresap founded what is now Oldtown, Maryland, by building a trading post.
The trading post stood at the foot of a Native American trail over Wills Mountain.
The article describes Wills Mountain as having been renamed Haystack and places it near Cresaptown.
The colonists wanted the Crown to open the Ohio Country lands to settlement.
The colonists wanted the lands to be granted by charter through the Crown's minister, as had been done before.
Cresap sent traders through the Cumberland Narrows pass.
Cresap personally explored Native American lands along the Monongahela upstream from Redstone Old Forts.
Maryland's land grant ended at the crest of the Appalachian Mountains.
Pennsylvania and Virginia both claimed that their land grants extended west of the Appalachian crest.
The lands that Cresap and his traders claimed west of the Appalachians ultimately became part of what the article calls upper West Virginia and western Pennsylvania.
Around 1744, some Native Americans claimed to sell their rights east of the Appalachians to Virginia land speculators.
The Ohio Company was a stock company involved in Virginia land speculation.
The Ohio Company received a charter around 1748.
The Ohio Company's charter covered two million acres.
The chartered lands lay in what are now western Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia.
Cresap received a large grant of Ohio Country land in what later became West Virginia.
Cresap served as an agent for the Ohio Company.
Nemacolin was a Delaware chief.
The expedition led by Cresap and Nemacolin began widening the Nemacolin Trail between 1748 and 1750.
The expedition aimed to make the trail suitable for freight wagons.
The improved route ran from Cumberland to Redstone Old Fort.
George Washington and his troops further improved the same road roughly a decade later.
Washington's improvements took place before Braddock's military expedition during the French and Indian War.
Redstone stood on the Monongahela River.
Redstone became Brownsville, Pennsylvania.
Brownsville outpaced Pittsburgh in growth and industrial activity until around the 1840s or 1850s, according to the article.
Brownsville became a center for building and outfitting river craft.
The river craft built or outfitted at Brownsville included keelboats, flatboats, and steamboats.
Settlers used such river craft to settle the Mississippi drainage basin.
Settlers also used such river craft on their way to the Far West and Oregon Country beyond the Missouri River's headwaters.
Cresap fought several skirmishes against Native Americans.
Cresap held his ground in the skirmishes with help from Hannah and, later, his sons.
Militia from Donegal surrounded Cresap's stronghold.
Hannah Cresap knew how to handle a musket.
Cresap forcibly took possession of John Hendricks's plantation.
Hendricks's plantation lay at what is now the upper end of Wrightsville.
While Cresap was away, Hannah supervised the construction of a house at the Hendricks property.
While Cresap was away, Hannah supervised the building of flatboats at the Hendricks property.
At the Hendricks property, Hannah saw a flatboat full of armed men crossing the river.
Hannah mounted a horse and sounded a bugle after seeing the armed men.
Hannah rode rapidly to Cresap's fort three and a half miles downriver.
Hannah returned at the head of the militia.
Cresap was elected to represent Frederick County in the Maryland legislature.
The French and their allies tried to take the territory west of the Allegheny Mountains from the English.
Cresap and his sons raised two companies of volunteers in response to the French and allied effort.
The Cresaps paid the expense of raising the two volunteer companies themselves.
Cresap raised a company of Rangers during the French and Indian War.
Cresap became completely blind a few years before his death.
Cresap's second wife was Margaret Milburn.
Cresap was 80 when he married Margaret Milburn.
Cresap died around 1790.
Cresap died at his home in Allegany County, Maryland.
The article gives Cresap's age at death as 88.
Thomas and Hannah Cresap had five children.
Thomas and Hannah's children included three sons and two daughters.
Daniel Cresap was Thomas and Hannah's eldest son.
Daniel Cresap remained in Washington County, Maryland.
Daniel Cresap became a large landowner.
Daniel Cresap was a farmer.
Daniel Cresap was a celebrated hunter.
Daniel Cresap was about 14 when the family left York County.
Daniel Cresap became a militia colonel as an adult.
Daniel Cresap had a son named Michael by his first wife.
The article says Daniel Cresap had seven sons and three daughters by his second wife.
The article names Daniel, Joseph, Van, Robert, James, Thomas, Elizabeth, Mary, and Sarah as children of Daniel Cresap's second marriage.
Daniel Cresap's son Daniel marched to Boston in his uncle Michael's company in 1775.
Daniel Cresap's son James served for several years in the Maryland legislature.
Thomas was Colonel Cresap's second son.
Colonel Cresap's son Thomas was killed by a Native American whom he killed at the same time.
Colonel Cresap's son Thomas left a widow and one child.
Colonel Cresap's son Michael was born on June 29, 1742.
Michael Cresap was born in Frederick County, Maryland.
Michael Cresap succeeded his father in the trade with Native Americans.
Michael Cresap ran a large trading store at Old Town, a few miles east of Cumberland.
Michael Cresap fought Native Americans from his youth.
In 1774, Michael Cresap hired several men and traveled down the Ohio River.
Michael Cresap and his men built houses and cleared land for settlers.
While Michael was working for settlers, Dr. Connolly warned him by letter that a war with Native Americans might break out.
Dr. Connolly commanded Fort Pitt.
The warning of a possible war alarmed settlers.
Michael Cresap and his party expected a Native American attack and struck first.
Some of Michael Cresap's men killed several Native Americans near Wheeling.
Soon afterward, a separate group of frontiersmen killed Logan's family and several other people.
Daniel Greathouse led the group that killed Logan's family.
Michael Cresap was wrongly accused of leading the killing of Logan's family.
Logan was a well-known Native American figure.
Logan reacted quickly to the killings by attacking frontier settlers.
Lord Dunmore's War followed the frontier violence.
The Battle of Point Pleasant took place along the Ohio River.
The Battle of Point Pleasant brought about a peace treaty.
Michael Cresap was held in esteem by his neighbors.
Michael Cresap was the first person in Maryland to raise a company of volunteer riflemen.
Michael Cresap led his rifle company to Boston in 1775.
The article describes Michael Cresap as fighting bravely at Boston.
Michael Cresap fell ill, possibly with tuberculosis.
Michael Cresap's illness forced him to return to New York.
Michael Cresap died in New York.
Michael Cresap was buried in Trinity Church Cemetery.
Michael Cresap left five children.
Michael Cresap's children included two sons and three daughters.

question.text: What was Thomas Cresap known for in colonial Maryland?
quotes: was an English-born Maryland settler, trader and land agent
was an English-born Maryland settler and trader
